state.misconception_label: Adds when calculating volume instead of multiplying

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The volume of this cuboid is \( 30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \) What length should replace the star? ![A cuboid, depth 2cm and height 3cm. The width is labelled with a star.](). I got \( 25 \mathrm{~cm} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain how you arrived at \(25 \mathrm{~cm}\) as the length to replace the star in the cuboid? What operation did you use to calculate the volume in this case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I added the height and the depth together, so \(3 \, \text{cm} + 2 \, \text{cm} = 5 \, \text{cm}\), and then I thought I needed to make it equal to \(30 \, \text{cm}^3\), so I just did \(30 \, \text{cm}^3 - 5 \, \text{cm} = 25 \, \text{cm}\). But now I'm not sure if I should have multiplied instead. Can you explain how the volume should really be calculated?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think about why adding the dimensions together might not give you the correct volume in this case? What operation do you think would be more appropriate to use when calculating the volume of a cuboid?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess adding the dimensions together doesn't really make sense for volume because volume is about how much space something takes up, right? I think maybe I should be multiplying the height, depth, and width instead. But I'm still a bit confused about how to set it up to find the width. Can you help me with that?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively engages with the addition misconception and the student shows clear progress toward understanding multiplication for volume, though the teacher could have provided more concrete scaffolding when the student explicitly requested help with setting up the equation in Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student toward discovering the correct approach without ever directly providing the answer or formula, which is a textbook example of the Socratic method.
